successor: Egypt - New Kingdom (18th Dynasty of Ahmose I, continuing the Theban 17th-dynasty kingship)
source1: Editors of Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Kamose', Encyclopaedia Britannica - https://www.britannica.com/biography/Kamose
source2: Editors of Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Ahmose I', Encyclopaedia Britannica - https://www.britannica.com/biography/Ahmose-I ; also UCL Digital Egypt, 'Egypt in the Second Intermediate Period' - https://www.ucl.ac.uk/museums-static/digitalegypt/2inter/index.html
notes: Theban 17th-dynasty king Kamose, at war with the Hyksos, was succeeded by his brother Ahmose, who took Avaris, reunited Egypt and founded the 18th dynasty: Theban authority continued unbroken. Database 1567 BCE reflects older chronology (c.1550/1539).

successor: Shabana (Shbanat) chief Abd al-Karim ibn Abi Bakr ash-Shbani in Marrakesh (1659-1668); then Alawi Sultanate (Marrakesh taken 1669)
source1: Editors of Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Sa'di dynasty', Encyclopaedia Britannica - https://www.britannica.com/topic/Sadi-dynasty
source2: Kingdom of Morocco official portal, 'History of Morocco: important dates' (1658/1659 entry) - https://maroc.ma/en/history-of-morocco/important-dates?page=8 ; also Britannica, 'al-Rashid' - https://www.britannica.com/biography/al-Rashid
notes: After the 1603 succession war the realm fragmented; Saadis kept Marrakesh. In 1659 the last sultan died and Marrakesh pledged allegiance to ash-Shbani, his maternal-kin army chief (internal takeover). Alawites (internal, Tafilalt) took Marrakesh 1669.

successor: French Kingdom - Late Bourbon (personal rule of Louis XIV)
source1: Editors of Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'The Fronde' (summary), Encyclopaedia Britannica - https://www.britannica.com/summary/The-Fronde
source2: Sara E. Chapman, 'Mazarin, Jules', Europe 1450 to 1789: Encyclopedia of the Early Modern World (Scribner/Gale, 2004), via Encyclopedia.com - https://www.encyclopedia.com/people/history/french-history-biographies/jules-mazarin
notes: Database split is a relabelling: Louis XIV reigned continuously from 1643; Mazarin's death (March 1661) began his personal rule within the same monarchy. The Fronde civil wars (1648-53) count as internal crisis. No break in central authority.

successor: Hotaki (Ghilzai Afghan) regime of Mahmud at Isfahan
notes: Ghilzai of Safavid Qandahar revolted under Mir Ways (1709); Mahmud besieged and took Isfahan 1722 and Sultan Husayn submitted. Rebels were subjects inside the realm, so internal per brief. Nominal Safavid restoration under Nader 1729-36.

successor: Babylonian kingship under Mar-biti-apla-usur ('Elamite dynasty', 984-979 BCE)
source1: RIBo (Royal Inscriptions of Babylonia online), LMU Munich, 'Babylon 4' (Bazi dynasty) and 'Babylon 5' (Mar-biti-apla-usur) - https://oracc.museum.upenn.edu/ribo/babylon4/ ; https://oracc.museum.upenn.edu/ribo/babylon5/
source2: Dynastic Chronicle (ABC 18), translation adapted from A.K. Grayson, Assyrian and Babylonian Chronicles (J.J. Augustin, 1975), Livius - https://www.livius.org/sources/content/mesopotamian-chronicles-content/abc-18-dynastic-chronicle/
notes: Bazi dynasty (c.1004-985 BCE, 20 years 3 months) was followed by Mar-biti-apla-usur, 'descendant of Elam', king of Babylon six years; no record of invasion, kingship continued. Mode inferred from king-list and chronicle only; evidence thin.

source1: Trenton Barnes, 'Teotihuacan', Heilbrunn Timeline of Art History, Metropolitan Museum of Art (2024) - https://www.metmuseum.org/toah/hd/teot/hd_teot.htm
source2: Martha L. Sempowski, 'Teotihuacan', Encyclopedia of Latin American History and Culture, via Encyclopedia.com - https://www.encyclopedia.com/humanities/encyclopedias-almanacs-transcripts-and-maps/teotihuacan
notes: Archaeological phase. Teotihuacan grew continuously from c.100 BCE into the Classic (monuments c.100-250 CE), absorbing most Basin population through planned resettlement; the phase boundary marks settlement continuity, not a break. Cuicuilco's burial by lava shifted population within the basin.

successor: Mongol Empire (Batu), then Golden Horde suzerainty
source1: Editors of Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Kyiv: History', Encyclopaedia Britannica - https://www.britannica.com/place/Kyiv/History
source2: Internet Encyclopedia of Ukraine (CIUS), 'Golden Horde' (from Encyclopedia of Ukraine vol. 2, 1989) and 'Mongols' - http://www.encyclopediaofukraine.com/display.asp?linkpath=pages%5CG%5CO%5CGoldenHorde.htm
notes: Rus split into feuding principalities that sapped Kyiv's power (sacked 1169); Batu's Mongols besieged and destroyed Kyiv in 1240, and Rus principalities became vassals of the Golden Horde (founded c.1242). Database 1242 reflects Horde founding.

successor: Neo-Assyrian Empire (Tiglath-pileser III as king of Babylon), after brief usurpation by Ukin-zer (Nabu-mukin-zeri) 731-729
source1: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Mesopotamia, history of: The Neo-Assyrian Empire (746-609)' - https://www.britannica.com/place/Mesopotamia-historical-region-Asia/The-Neo-Assyrian-Empire-746-609
notes: Nabonassar's death (734) brought chaos and usurpations; Ukin-zer crowned himself; Tiglath-pileser III beat him (731), captured him 729 and took the Babylonian crown himself. Database 732 ends the king-list dynasty, not the state.

successor: Ottoman Empire (Buda entered 1526, Zapolya installed as vassal, Buda annexed 1541)
source1: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Hungary: The period of partition' - https://www.britannica.com/place/Hungary/The-period-of-partition
source2: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Battle of Mohacs' - https://www.britannica.com/event/Battle-of-Mohacs ; and 'Hungary: The Jagiellon kings: National decay' - https://www.britannica.com/place/Hungary/The-Jagiellon-kings-National-decay
notes: Ottomans annihilated the army at Mohacs 1526; Louis II died; Suleyman entered Buda. Double election and civil war followed; Zapolya was installed in Buda as Ottoman vassal; Buda annexed 1541. Dozsa revolt 1514 was prior crisis.

successor: Lombard Kingdom (Aistulf), 751-756; then Republic of St Peter (papacy)
notes: Lombard king Aistulf conquered Ravenna in 751, ending Byzantine control; Pippin III took it from the Lombards and gave it to the pope (756-57). The exarchate was broken by revolts and invasions after 726. Database home area 'Latium' is misleading.
